physics.overview: Tree climbing and rigging rely heavily on physics. Understanding rope angles, friction, load distribution, and mechanical advantage makes you a safer and more efficient arborist.

ropePhysics.tension: Rope tension increases with load weight and rope angle.
ropePhysics.friction: Friction reduces force but increases heat. Devices manage friction safely.
ropePhysics.bendRadius: Sharp bends weaken rope. Use pulleys to maintain proper radius.
ropePhysics.stretch: Static ropes stretch less, providing predictable movement.

loadDistribution.weakPoints: Weak attachments can fail under stress.
loadDistribution.triangulation: Multiple anchors reduce load on any single point.
loadDistribution.compressionTension: Wood reacts differently depending on compression and tension.

mechanicalAdvantage.pulleys: Pulleys reduce friction and increase efficiency.
mechanicalAdvantage.redirects: Redirects change direction without changing mechanical advantage.

climbingMechanics.bodyThrust: Uses hips and legs to move upward efficiently.
climbingMechanics.footlocking: Locks rope between feet for controlled ascent.
climbingMechanics.ropeWalking: Uses ascenders to walk up rope smoothly.
climbingMechanics.SRS: Single rope systems provide efficient vertical movement.
climbingMechanics.MRS: Moving rope systems provide dynamic movement and control.

canopyPhysics.limbWalking: Balance and weight distribution are key.
canopyPhysics.sway: Trees sway to dissipate energy. Climbers must anticipate movement.
canopyPhysics.windLoad: Wind increases stress on limbs and anchors.
canopyPhysics.branchAngles: Branch angles determine strength and breakage risk.

riggingPhysics.negativeRigging: Loads move downward, increasing force on anchor.
riggingPhysics.speedlines: Speedlines use gravity to move wood quickly.
riggingPhysics.frictionDevices: Devices manage speed and prevent shock-loading.
riggingPhysics.shockLoad: Sudden force can break anchors or ropes.

cuttingPhysics.kickback: Kickback occurs when bar tip contacts wood.
